document.title: Pak Foreign Minister Asks U.S. Cooperation on Afghanistan
document.publisher: National Security Archive (GWU), The Taliban File
document.note: [Confidential] Acting Secretary Strobe Talbott tells Pakistani Foreign Minister Assef Ali that Pakistani support for the Taliban is forcing Moscow and Tehran to keep aiding Rabbani and Masoud. He draws an analogy between support for the Taliban and for Kashmiri militants, warning of unintended consequences.

events.description: Pakistani FM Assef Ali, with ISI DG Nasim Rana, met Acting Secretary Talbott for 70 minutes on Afghanistan policy coordination.
Attack on Pakistani embassy personnel and burning of the Pakistani embassy in Kabul.
State Department cable reporting the Talbott-Ali meeting.

Acting Secretary Talbott meets Pakistani Foreign Minister Ali, ISI DG Rana and Ambassador Lodhi on Afghanistan; Talbott urges Pakistan to return to neutrality and stop supporting the Taliban; Pakistan denies military aid.
Planned dinner in Helsinki between Secretary Christopher and Primakov to raise outside interference in Afghanistan.
Foreign Minister Ali's lunch with A/S Raphel on U.S. view of Russian aims.
Taliban forced down a Russian plane in Kandahar and held the aircrew; U.S. urged Pakistan to push for release.
Pakistani FM Assef Ali meets Acting Secretary Talbott for 70 minutes on Afghanistan, Kashmir, and nuclear issues.
Fatal attack on Pakistani personnel and burning of the Pakistani Embassy in Kabul.
Planned dinner in Helsinki between the Secretary and Primakov, where outside interference in Afghanistan was to be raised.
Taliban forced down a Russian plane in Kandahar and detained its aircrew.
Assef Ali lunches with A/S Raphel to discuss Russian aims in Central Asia and Afghanistan.

key_claims: Pakistani FM Ali categorically denied that Pakistan gave military assistance to the Taliban, admitting only phone lines, communication links and some Kandahar reconstruction funds.
ISI chief Nasim Rana claimed Pakistan gave 'not one bullet' to the Taliban.
Talbott argued that Russian, Iranian and Indian arms to Rabbani and Massoud were a backlash to Pakistani support for the Taliban, widely presumed to be backed by the U.S.
Pakistan said it tried to broker a Taliban-Dostum alliance to moderate the Taliban, whose beliefs are 'simple, rigid and antique' and who lack structure.
Ali alleged Iran has expansionist aims in western and northern Afghanistan and Russia needs Afghan instability to justify a military presence.
Talbott drew an analogy between Pakistani support for the Taliban and for Kashmiri militants, warning of uncontrollable unintended consequences such as kidnappings of foreigners.
The U.S. urged Pakistan to push the Taliban to release the Russian aircrew forced down in Kandahar.
